gaps.sentence: That's the boy ___ dog won first prize at the show.
gaps.hint: the dog belongs to the boy
gaps.explanation: 'Whose dog' means 'his dog'; 'who's' would mean 'who is', which makes no sense here.

gaps.sentence: It was the best meal ___ I have ever eaten.
gaps.hint: after a superlative, this pronoun is preferred
gaps.explanation: After superlatives ('the best ...'), 'that' is the preferred relative pronoun in defining clauses.

gaps.sentence: Students ___ hand in their essays late will lose marks.
gaps.explanation: 'Who' refers to the students performing the action; the verb 'will lose' follows later in the sentence.

gaps.sentence: This is the beach ___ we used to play as children.
gaps.explanation: 'Where' introduces place information; 'we used to play' already has a subject and object, so 'which' is impossible.

gaps.sentence: The book ___ I borrowed from the library is two weeks overdue.
gaps.explanation: 'Which' refers to things; 'who' refers only to people and 'where' to places.

gaps.sentence: He passed all his exams first time, ___ surprised everyone.
gaps.hint: refers to the whole previous clause
gaps.explanation: 'Which' can refer to a whole idea ('he passed first time'); this non-defining use never takes 'that'.

gaps.sentence: She told me ___ had happened, but I didn't believe her.
gaps.explanation: 'What had happened' means 'the things that had happened'; 'that' cannot stand alone as the subject here.

gaps.sentence: The new bridge, ___ cost two billion euros, opened last month.
gaps.hint: thing + extra information after a comma
gaps.explanation: 'Which' introduces non-defining clauses about things; 'that' is forbidden there.
